nodes.name: Hydrothermal MoS2 synthesis
nodes.procedure: MoS2 nanosheets were grown on carbon cloths by a hydrothermal method with ammonium molybdate tetrahydrate [(NH4)6Mo7O24·4H2O] and thiourea (CH4N2S) as the precursors.
nodes.source_text: MoS2 nanosheets were grown on carbon cloths by a hydrothermal method with ammonium molybdate tetrahydrate... and thiourea (CH4N2S) as the precursors.

nodes.name: NiFe LDH formation on MoS2
nodes.procedure: The obtained MoS2 nanosheets were immersed into a mixed solution of nickel acetate and ferrous sulfate to adsorb Fe and Ni ions onto the surface. After drying in air, the MoS2/NiFe LDH pre-catalysts were constructed.

nodes.name: Electrochemical Mo leaching
nodes.procedure: The MoS2/NiFe LDH pre-catalysts were subjected to cyclic voltammetry activation in 1 M KOH solution to obtain self-reconstruction Mo doping NiFe (oxy)hydroxide through Mo leaching.
nodes.source_text: The MoS2/NiFe LDH pre-catalysts were subjected to cyclic voltammetry activation in 1 M KOH solution to obtain self-reconstruction Mo doping NiFe (oxy)hydroxide through Mo leaching.

nodes.name: NiFe (oxy)hydroxide reference synthesis
nodes.procedure: The NiFe (oxy)hydroxide reference sample was synthesized by a commonly used wet-chemical method. Further detailed information about NiFe and MoNiFe (oxy)hydroxides synthesis can be found in Supplementary note 9, 10.
nodes.source_text: The NiFe (oxy)hydroxide reference sample was synthesized by a commonly used wet-chemical method.

nodes.characterization_summary: SEM shows that the (oxy)hydroxide layer uniformly covers the carbon fiber.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image (Fig. 1c) shows that the (oxy)hydroxide layer uniformly covers the carbon fiber.

nodes.characterization_summary: AFM shows ultrathin MoNiFe (oxy)hydroxide flakes with atomic thickness of 0.8 nm (monolayer) or 1.5 nm (double-layer).
nodes.evidence_snippet: The atomic force microscopy (AFM) results of the (oxy)hydroxide flake prepared by ultrasonic treatment suggest that the active catalyst was ultrathin with an atomic thickness of 0.8 nm (mono-layer, denoted as 1 L) or 1.5 nm (double-layer, denoted as 2 L) (Fig. 1d).

nodes.characterization_summary: ICP-OES determines Ni, Fe, and Mo contents of 48.7, 19.4, and 0.11 μg/cm² respectively, indicating 0.1% Mo doping.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Using inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES), the Ni, Fe, and Mo contents of the obtained catalyst were determined to be 48.7, 19.4, and 0.11 μg/cm², respectively, indicating a small concentration (0.1%) of Mo doping in MoNiFe-27% (oxy)hydroxide.

nodes.characterization_summary: HAADF-STEM confirms presence of Mo dopant in NiFe (oxy)hydroxide.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The presence of Mo dopant in NiFe (oxy)hydroxide was further confirmed by the aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscope (HAADF-STEM) (Supplementary Fig. 4).

nodes.characterization_summary: HRTEM shows lattice spacing of 0.2 nm assigned to (105) plane of oxyhydroxide; SAED exhibits diffraction rings of (101), (110) for Ni-based hydroxide and (105), (006) for Ni-based oxyhydroxide.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The spacing between two adjacent lattice planes is quantified to be 0.2 nm (Fig. 1f), which is assigned to the (105) plane of oxyhydroxide. The selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern of the (oxy)hydroxide in Fig. 1g exhibits clear diffraction rings of (101), (110) plane for Ni-based hydroxide (PDF-#14-0117) and (105), (006) plane for Ni-based oxyhydroxide (PDF-#06-0075).

nodes.characterization_summary: EDS mapping reveals uniform distribution of O, Fe, Ni, and Mo elements in MoNiFe (oxy)hydroxide.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) mapping revealed the uniform distribution of O, Fe, Ni, and Mo elements in MoNiFe (oxy)hydroxide (Fig. 1h).

nodes.characterization_summary: O K-edge sXAS shows decreased intensity after Mo doping indicating weakened metal-oxygen hybridization; Ni L-edge and Fe L-edge show increased intensity and shifts indicating higher metal oxidation states.
nodes.evidence_snippet: O K-edge, Ni L-edge, and Fe L-edge soft X-ray absorption spectroscopies (sXAS) of NiFe and MoNiFe (oxy)hydroxide.

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS confirms higher metal oxidation state in MoNiFe (oxy)hydroxide and higher content of defective oxygen.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The structure and composition of MoNiFe (oxy)hydroxide catalyst remain unchanged after the long-time operation, as revealed by SEM, TEM, EDS, XPS, and ICP-OES characterizations (Supplementary Fig. 13-17).

nodes.characterization_summary: In-situ Raman shows delayed Ni²⁺/Ni³⁺ redox transition at higher potential (1.450 V vs RHE) for MoNiFe compared to NiFe (1.414 V vs RHE); Ni³⁺-O peaks emerge at 0.48 V vs Hg/HgO for MoNiFe vs 0.44 V for NiFe; faster oxygen exchange observed in ¹⁸O-labeled MoNiFe.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Ni²⁺/Ni³⁺ redox peak for MoNiFe (oxy)hydroxide (1.450 V vs. RHE) shifted positively compared to that of NiFe (oxy)hydroxide (1.414 V vs. RHE)... The emergence of the Raman peaks of Ni³⁺-O occurred at 0.44 V and 0.48 V (vs. Hg/HgO) for NiFe and MoNiFe (oxy)hydroxide, respectively.
